edges.description: The model reproduces the full biochemical lesion, and the study attributes the neuronal damage specifically to elevated sulfite rather than to cofactor absence in the abstract.
edges.limitations: The abstract reports the metabolite changes as a set rather than individually, so it does not by itself quantify S-sulfocysteine in the mouse.

edges.description: The lethal early-postnatal encephalopathic course is reproduced, and microarray analysis shows a cell-death program in brain.
edges.limitations: Morphological brain damage was explicitly excluded in the mouse, so the model captures the secondary apoptotic injury but not the structural findings - cerebellar hypoplasia, thin corpus callosum, cystic encephalomalacia - that dominate human MRI. Mouse survival is measured in days to two weeks against a human course running into infancy, so the model compresses the timeline the treatment-window question turns on.

nodes.description: Four molybdoenzymes exist in humans, and all of them lose activity together: sulfite oxidase, xanthine oxidoreductase, aldehyde oxidase and the mitochondrial amidoxime-reducing component. The name of the disease - combined deficiency of sulfite oxidase, xanthine dehydrogenase and aldehyde oxidase - records this. What the name does not record is that the deficiencies are not clinically equal, which the next two nodes separate.
nodes.id: Absent Molybdenum Cofactor and Combined Molybdoenzyme Failure

evidence.snippet: There are two cytosolic Mo-enzymes, xanthine oxidoreductase and aldehyde oxidase, which are closely related Mo-iron-flavin enzymes catalyzing the hydroxylation reactions of purines and various heterocyclic substrates

meta.association: Biallelic MOCS1 variants cause molybdenum cofactor deficiency type A, the commonest of the three complementation groups. MOCS1 is transcribed as both a bicistronic and a monocistronic mRNA through alternative splicing, encoding the two proteins that together catalyze GTP to cyclic pyranopterin monophosphate. Genotype does not distinguish type A clinically - only molecularly - but it determines eligibility for the only targeted therapy that exists.

evidence.snippet: The majority of mutations leading to MoCo deficiency have been identified in the genes MOCS1 (type A deficiency), MOCS2 (type B deficiency), with one reported in GPHN
MOCS1 expression undergoes alternative splicing, yielding two different types of transcripts, one bicistronic and one monocistronic mRNA

nodes.description: The initiating lesion, and its position in the pathway is what makes this subtype treatable. Molybdenum cofactor is built in three steps by the products of MOCS1, MOCS2, MOCS3 and GPHN. MOCS1 catalyzes the first of them, the conversion of GTP into cyclic pyranopterin monophosphate. A block at step one leaves every downstream step intact and starved of substrate - which is precisely the situation a substrate can be given back into.

evidence.snippet: The first step in Moco biosynthesis, the conversion of GTP into cPMP, is catalyzed by two proteins encoded by the MOCS1 locus
Moco is synthesized by a three-step biosynthetic pathway that involves the gene products of MOCS1, MOCS2, MOCS3, and GPHN

nodes.description: The type A model. Homozygous Mocs1-null mice reproduce the enzyme and metabolite changes seen in patients, die within about two weeks of birth, and were the system in which substrate replacement with a biosynthetic Moco precursor - the strategy that became fosdenopterin - was first shown to work. Detailed analysis found no morphological brain damage but a massive transcriptional cell-death program, triggered by elevated sulfite and delayed in utero by maternal clearance, which is why affected pups are born well and decompensate after birth.

evidence.snippet: We have recently described a murine model for Moco-deficiency, which reflects all enzyme and metabolite changes observed in the patients, and an efficient therapy using a biosynthetic precursor of Moco has been established in this animal model

nodes.description: Presentation in the first days of life with severe encephalopathy - refractory seizures, opisthotonos, axial and appendicular hypotonia, feeding difficulty and apnea - with imaging showing loss of grey-white differentiation, gyral swelling and panlobar diffusion restriction through the forebrain and midbrain, characteristically sparing the brain stem. The injury is largely complete by the time it is recognized, which is the central fact governing treatment.

animal_models.description: The lethal early-postnatal encephalopathic course is reproduced, and microarray analysis shows a cell-death program in brain.
animal_models.name: Mocs1-null mouse (Moco-deficient mouse)

evidence.snippet: Individuals with early-onset MoCD typically present in the first days of life with severe encephalopathy, including refractory seizures, opisthotonos, axial and appendicular hypotonia, feeding difficulties, and apnea
panlobar diffusion restriction throughout the forebrain and midbrain with relative sparring of the brain stem

nodes.description: Survivors have profound developmental delay, truncal hypotonia and limb hypertonia evolving into spastic quadriplegia or diplegia, acquired microcephaly and dysmorphic features. Mortality is high and early: about a quarter of neonatal-onset type A patients die before their first birthday, and the median age at death is 2.4 years.
nodes.id: Profound Neurodevelopmental Disability and Early Mortality

evidence.snippet: Sequelae included profound developmental delay, truncal hypotonia, limb hypertonia that evolved to spastic quadriplegia or diplegia, dysmorphic features, and acquired microcephaly
One-year survival rates were 77.4% (overall), 71.8% (neonatal onset MoCD-A), and 76.9% (neonatal onset MoCD-B); median ages at death were 2.4, 2.4, and 2.2 years, respectively
The median survival for the overall population was 36 months

nodes.description: Xanthine oxidoreductase converts hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to urate, so its loss raises xanthine and lowers urate. This arm is curated separately from the sulfite arm because it behaves differently: it produces the biochemical signature that makes the diagnosis - high xanthine with a urate below the reference range - while contributing little of the clinical disease. A patient with isolated xanthinuria has kidney stones, not a neonatal encephalopathy.

evidence.snippet: In MoCD-A and MoCD-B, plasma and urinary xanthine and S-sulfocysteine concentrations were high; urate remained below the normal reference range

nodes.description: The step that converts a metabolic block into neuronal death. S-sulfocysteine is a structural analog of glutamate, and it activates NMDA-type glutamate receptors, admitting calcium and triggering downstream signalling including calpain activation. This is why the encephalopathy is destructive rather than merely dysfunctional, and why the neonatal window is so narrow.

evidence.snippet: SSC represents a structural analog of glutamate and has been proven to cause excitotoxicity in neurons by activating N-methyl-D-aspartate type glutamate (NMDA) receptors, causing calcium influx and downstream signaling such as calpain activation
The effects of these S-sulfonated species remain largely unknown except for S-sulfocysteine (SSC)

nodes.description: Sulfite oxidase normally converts sulfite to sulfate at the end of cysteine catabolism. Without it sulfite accumulates and drives secondary chemistry: S-sulfocysteine and thiosulfate rise while cysteine and cystine fall. This is the arm that produces the clinical disease. The evidence for that is comparative rather than direct - isolated sulfite oxidase deficiency, in which only this one enzyme is lost, reproduces almost the whole phenotype.

animal_models.description: The model reproduces the full biochemical lesion, and the study attributes the neuronal damage specifically to elevated sulfite rather than to cofactor absence in the abstract.
animal_models.name: Mocs1-null mouse (Moco-deficient mouse)

evidence.snippet: The molecular cause of the disease is the loss of sulfite oxidase (SOX) activity, one of four Moco-dependent enzymes in men
Accumulating toxic sulfite causes a secondary increase of metabolites such as S-sulfocysteine and thiosulfate as well as a decrease in cysteine and its oxidized form, cystine
Most of the symptoms in MoCD patients are mirrored by iSOD, which is caused by mutations in the SUOX gene
